video_title: Lawfare Daily: Ukraine, Iran, Taiwan, and the Short War Illusion
gist: A Lawfare panel (Carnegie's Dara on Russia/Eurasia, the Chicago Council's Ari, and a 25-year CIA veteran, Julia) applies Kathleen Nolan's 'short war illusion' framework -- decapitation, chokepoint denial, protraction -- to Russia-Ukraine and the US/Israel-Iran conflict, then extrapolates the lessons Beijing is drawing for a Taiwan invasion: a 2027 PLA capability deadline, cost-asymmetric denial weapons (cheap drones and mines vs. million-dollar interceptors), and Western stockpile shortfalls (Patriot interceptors) that are already constraining support to Ukraine and could similarly hamstring a Taiwan intervention.

insights.claim: Kathleen Nolan's 'short war illusion' framework describes how aggressor states repeatedly convince themselves a war of choice will be short, sharp and decisive, then discover it becomes a long war of attrition; the framework breaks into three phases -- decapitation (an opening decisive strike meant to paralyze the enemy), chokepoint denial (the defender imposing outsized costs at critical nodes), and protraction (a drawn-out war of endurance once the first two fail).
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Gives investors a repeatable lens to score any live or emerging conflict (Ukraine, Iran, Taiwan) on which phase it's in and how likely early 'quick win' state narratives are to be wrong -- useful for pricing escalation and duration risk.

insights.claim: Historically, states that launch short-war strategies and lose the gamble include Germany before both World Wars, Japan before World War II, and repeatedly the USSR/Russia (Afghanistan, Chechnya, Georgia 2008, Crimea 2014), suggesting the illusion is a structural bias in authoritarian and revisionist military planning rather than a one-off miscalculation.
insights.speaker: Julia / Dara
insights.so_what: A base-rate for handicapping any new short-war bet (including a future Taiwan invasion) -- the historical pattern favors protraction over quick capitulation, which should discount scenarios pricing a fast resolution.

insights.claim: Russia's 2022 invasion plan assumed a decapitation strike on Kyiv, the assassination of Zelensky, and a Russian-installed 'shadow government' of pre-recruited Ukrainian officials at municipal, state and federal level would make Ukrainians lay down arms without a fight, mirroring Russia's successful bloodless 2014 seizure of Crimea.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: Illustrates how a prior tactical success (Crimea 2014) can become a dangerously miscalibrated template for a much larger operation -- a pattern worth watching for other revisionist actors extrapolating from limited past wins.
insights.quote: They thought if they decapitated or assassinated Zalinsky and they showed up with their tanks that the Ukrainians would see them and just stop fighting.

insights.claim: Ukraine's SBU/security services arrested 600-700 people in the shadow-government network in the days before the 2022 invasion, gutting Russia's plan to install a puppet government, while other paid Russian collaborators simply failed to show up once the invasion began going badly.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A concrete counterintelligence data point showing how thin and penetrable Russia's pre-war political infrastructure inside Ukraine actually was -- relevant to assessing how much stock to put in claims of fifth-column readiness in other theaters (e.g., China/Taiwan).

insights.claim: Russia's pre-invasion closed-door polling reportedly suggested Ukrainian public sentiment was roughly 50/50 on whether to fight back, a small-sample and badly wrong estimate that fed directly into the decapitation plan.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: Shows how closed autocratic decision loops can rely on low-quality intelligence/polling to justify high-stakes military bets -- a warning sign to watch for in other closed regimes (China) making similar irreversible calls.

insights.claim: Russia's 2022 invasion plan had no branch/contingency plan ('plan B') for what to do if the rapid road-march-and-decapitation approach failed within the first few days, leaving the campaign improvised and reactive once the initial assumptions collapsed.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A concrete planning failure (no contingency branch) that turned a battlefield setback into a strategic rout -- a specific checklist item for assessing how brittle any other state's invasion plan (e.g. China's Taiwan plan) might be.

insights.claim: CIA Director Bill Burns's warning to Moscow that the West would get materially involved if Russia invaded Ukraine was accurate, but the Kremlin dismissed it as a bluff -- a misjudgment about how deep US/Western involvement would actually go.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: Highlights a recurring risk in deterrence signaling: adversaries can hear an accurate warning and still discount it, meaning explicit pre-crisis signaling to China over Taiwan may face the same credibility problem.
insights.quote: when Bill Burns went to Moscow and told them, "We're going to get involved. We, the West, are going to get involved," that he was telling the truth. He wasn't making that up.

insights.claim: Russia has repeated the same decapitation/quick-capitulation mistake roughly every 5-10 years across Afghanistan, Chechnya, Georgia, and Ukraine (2014 and 2022) without institutionally internalizing the lesson, because admitting the failure is politically dangerous within a closed, Putin-centered decision structure.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: Suggests Russia is structurally unlikely to self-correct this planning bias, which matters for forecasting how a future Russian move (e.g., against a NATO frontier state) might again start from flawed short-war assumptions.

themes.theme: The US/Israel-Iran conflict: decapitation and shifting objectives

insights.claim: The Trump administration's decapitation strategy against Iran -- striking the Supreme Leader and senior IRGC commanders in hopes the regime would collapse -- was partly shaped by the prior year's 'Operation Midnight Hammer' (the '12-day war') against Iran's nuclear program, which ended without major escalation and wrongly reinforced the view that a fast, contained campaign was repeatable.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A precedent-driven planning error: a prior limited success created false confidence for a much larger, riskier bet -- the same pattern Dara identified for Russia's Crimea-to-Ukraine leap.

insights.claim: The 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War is the clearest historical analog for the current Iran conflict: Saddam Hussein invaded a post-revolutionary, hostage-crisis-weakened Iran expecting a quick annexation of oil-rich, Arab-minority border regions, and instead got an eight-year war with hundreds of thousands of deaths and chemical-weapons use that left both countries roughly where they started.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A directly on-point historical base rate the US administration reportedly failed to weight properly -- underscores the risk of discounting an adversary's demonstrated willingness to absorb catastrophic losses rather than capitulate.

insights.claim: The US administration underestimated Iran's resilience and overestimated US tactical/operational superiority, not recognizing that Iran has spent decades building a military doctrine specifically designed to deter and fight a technologically superior adversary cheaply and asymmetrically.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: Signals that low-cost asymmetric doctrines (relevant to Iran, and by extension any US near-peer competitor) can neutralize a large conventional/technological edge -- a key variable for handicapping any future US intervention scenario, including Taiwan.

insights.claim: US war aims against Iran shifted repeatedly over the campaign -- from full regime change, to fostering internal uprising, to destroying nuclear capability, to (once full nuclear rollback proved unattainable) degrading missile and drone sites -- undermining coherent military planning because the political objective kept moving.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: Objective drift is itself a leading indicator of protraction risk and mission failure -- a useful early tell for investors trying to gauge how long a conflict with unclear political end-states will run.
insights.quote: the the objectives kept shifting, they're still in some ways shifting. And so it makes it really hard to actually be able to plan if you don't know what you're trying to achieve at the end of the day.

insights.claim: Israel's strikes reportedly also targeted Iranian reform-minded opposition figures inside the regime (some under house arrest for years/decades) who could have plausibly led an advantageous leadership transition, undercutting any coherent US/Israeli plan for what would follow a successful decapitation.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A specific execution flaw showing coalition partners (US/Israel) pursued misaligned sub-objectives even within a single campaign -- a risk factor for any multilateral intervention, including a hypothetical US-allied Taiwan defense.

insights.claim: The US/Israel had no agreed post-strike transition plan for Iran -- competing candidates for a successor government were floated and then publicly disavowed by the president mid-conflict -- meaning the campaign proceeded without the pre-war planning work regime-change operations typically require.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A repeatable diagnostic for judging the credibility of any stated 'regime change' objective in a live conflict: absence of a real succession plan is a strong signal of improvisation and prolonged instability risk.

themes.theme: China/Taiwan: the decapitation plan and the 2027 deadline

insights.claim: Xi Jinping has reportedly set 2027 as the deadline for the PLA to have the capability to invade and take Taiwan specifically in the face of US intervention; without US intervention, no one doubts China can already defeat Taiwan, so PLA modernization has focused overwhelmingly on speed and anti-access/area-denial (A2AD) capability to keep the US out before it can act.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: A concrete, datable capability deadline that markets and defense-sector investors can anchor scenario planning to for Taiwan-conflict tail risk and related semiconductor/supply-chain exposure.
insights.quote: Xiinping has given his military until 2027 a significant anniversary of of note for for China to have the capability to invade Taiwan specifically in the face of US intervention.

insights.claim: China's primary opening-move plan for a Taiwan invasion, mirroring Russia in Ukraine and the US/Israel in Iran, is a decapitation strike on Taiwan's political leadership (via hypersonic and ballistic missile capability) intended to induce paralysis and prevent organized resistance, followed by a march into Taipei or negotiation with whoever remains.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Confirms the expected opening signature of a Taiwan contingency (missile/hypersonic strikes on leadership targets) as the tripwire event investors and governments would need to watch for.

insights.claim: China has built full-scale mockup buildings in mainland China -- including a replica of the Taiwanese presidential palace, observed via commercial satellite imagery -- to let PLA special forces regularly war-game capturing or killing Taiwan's leadership.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: A verifiable, satellite-observable indicator of PLA invasion-rehearsal intensity that intelligence and OSINT-following investors can monitor over time as a leading indicator of readiness.
insights.quote: have built uh mockup buildings in mainland China that commercial satellites have observed of of you know a mockup of the presidential palace of the president of Taiwan and they can regularly war game with their special forces

insights.claim: Having watched decapitation strategies fail twice in quick succession (Russia in Ukraine, the US/Israel in Iran), Beijing is expected to hedge beyond a single opening decapitation strike by investing further in fifth-column operations, bribing Taiwanese officials/military to defect or stand down, and cyberattacks meant to paralyze Taiwanese civil society alongside any physical opening strike.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Suggests the Taiwan threat picture is broadening beyond a single kinetic tripwire toward hybrid pre-invasion subversion (cyber, bribery, fifth column) -- relevant for Taiwanese and allied cybersecurity/critical-infrastructure hardening investment theses.

themes.theme: Chokepoint denial economics: Ukraine, Iran, and the Taiwan read-through

insights.claim: Because Russia's invasion routes had been compromised to Western/Ukrainian intelligence before 2022, Ukraine was able to create literal chokepoints on Russian advance roads, attriting Russia's most trained soldiers and modern equipment early in the war and forcing Russia to abandon roughly half its territorial objectives, including the assault on Kyiv, within a few months.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: Demonstrates how compromised operational plans plus prepared chokepoint defenses can convert an opening offensive rout into a strategic-level failure -- a template for assessing Taiwan's own chokepoint/urban defense potential.

insights.claim: Ukrainian deep-strike drone and missile campaigns have disrupted an estimated 30-40% of Russia's oil and gas industry, which Dara calls 'astronomical,' yet this level of damage has still not been sufficient to compel Russia to halt the war.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A hard data point on how much energy-sector damage a determined adversary can absorb without capitulating -- relevant for calibrating how much economic/energy pressure would actually be needed to coerce a large petrostate.
insights.quote: It's disrupted 30 to 40% of Russia's oil and gas industry, which is astronomical. It's still not causing them to stop.

insights.claim: Russia's war economy and military supply chain are being sustained by external partners in ways sanctions haven't cut off: China provides broad economic/industrial support without which the war 'would not be possible,' Iran supplied the Shahed drone IP that Russia now domestically produces as the 'Geran' variant, and North Korea has supplied artillery, rockets and troops, notably at Kursk.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: Maps the multilateral sanctions-evasion supply chain keeping Russia's war machine running -- directly relevant to sanctions-regime design and to gauging China-Russia-Iran-North Korea alignment as a durable geopolitical bloc.

insights.claim: Because Western/allied Patriot interceptor stockpiles are running short, Russia is deliberately shifting its offensive from a stalled ground war (both sides suppressed by drone saturation) toward an accelerating ballistic-missile strike campaign against Kyiv, betting that Ukraine's air defenses cannot be sustained at current levels.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A live, trackable indicator (Patriot stock levels and Kyiv strike tempo) that signals where the Russia-Ukraine war is likely to intensify next, with direct relevance to US/European air-defense production and export-priority decisions.

insights.claim: In the Iran-Iraq War era, a single Iranian contact mine estimated to cost about $1,500 crippled a US frigate, requiring 18 months and roughly $100 million to repair -- an extreme cost asymmetry that still defines naval-mine and cheap-drone threats today.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: A concrete historical ROI figure for denial weapons vs. platform cost -- directly transferable to modeling China's or Taiwan's mine/drone-based denial economics in a strait conflict, and to naval procurement/insurance risk pricing.
insights.quote: an Iranian contact mine, which which estimated to have cost at one point $1,500, crippled a US frigot, you know, in the Iran Iraq war time frame. It took 18 months to repair and $100 million of of damage.

insights.claim: Iranian-derived one-way-attack drones (Shahed-style, now also used against Ukraine) cost roughly $20,000-$50,000 each, while a sophisticated modern interceptor to shoot one down costs in the millions of dollars with limited magazine depth -- a cost/inventory mismatch that Julia says should make Chinese planners 'very nervous' Taiwan will adopt the same denial defense against an amphibious invasion.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Direct read-through for defense-industrial investment theses: cheap mass drones/mines vs. expensive precision interceptors is an economics problem facing any modern navy in a strait denial scenario, favoring low-cost mass-production defense suppliers over exquisite single-unit interceptor programs.

insights.claim: The PLA is actively working to close its own denial-weapon vulnerability gap by building unmanned mine-sweeping naval vehicles (to avoid relying solely on manned minesweepers) and self-propelled 'water bridge' barges modeled on the WWII D-Day Mulberry harbors, designed to create makeshift docks on Taiwanese shorelines and compress the time needed to punch through layered coastal defenses -- though Julia says China remains 'a long way' from solving the problem.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Specific PLA hardware programs (unmanned mine-sweepers, D-Day-style barges) are trackable procurement/OSINT signals of amphibious-invasion readiness timelines relevant to defense-sector and Taiwan-risk monitoring.

themes.theme: Iran's asymmetric chokepoint playbook: Hormuz and the proxy network

insights.claim: Because Iran cannot strike the US homeland the way the US can strike Iran, and because it faces a conventionally superior, nuclear-armed adversary backed by a regional alliance network, Iran built its entire deterrence and war-fighting doctrine around two asymmetric levers: weaponizing freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and leveraging its network of non-state partners and proxy forces across the region to hold US installations and personnel at risk.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A clear two-lever framework (chokepoint threat + proxy network) for anticipating how Iran will respond to future escalation, with direct implications for oil-shipping risk premia and Gulf energy infrastructure insurance/security spend.

insights.claim: Iran deliberately targeted Gulf energy-sector installations, infrastructure and tourism assets belonging to US regional partners specifically because Iran knew these targets would raise the economic and political cost of the conflict fastest, aiming to pressure Washington indirectly through its allies rather than through direct confrontation.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: Identifies Gulf energy and tourism infrastructure as the specific pressure points Iran will target again in any renewed escalation -- a direct signal for energy-infrastructure risk hedging and regional insurance/reinsurance pricing.

insights.claim: Iran's strategy leans on the fact that any US administration operates under a fixed political calendar (e.g., the approaching midterms) that authoritarian Iran does not face in the same way, giving Tehran an inherent patience advantage in any war of endurance with Washington.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A structural asymmetry (democratic electoral clock vs. authoritarian indefinite horizon) that should be priced into any assumption about how long the US can sustain costly foreign engagements before domestic political pressure forces de-escalation.

themes.theme: Defense industrial base as the real center of gravity

insights.claim: The US administration frames degrading Iran's missile and drone programs as a durable win regardless of how the war ends, but Ari argues this overstates the achievement because these are deliberately unsophisticated, cheap, and easy-to-rebuild capabilities -- Russia, for example, rapidly ramped up domestic production of Iranian-derived Shahed drones early in the Ukraine war.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: Warns against overweighting 'capability degradation' as a lasting strategic win when the underlying technology is cheap and quickly reconstitutable -- a caution for assessing claimed 'victories' in any sanctions/strike-based deterrence campaign.

insights.claim: US and allied defense industrial base output and stockpiles (Patriot, HIMARS and other interceptor/munitions systems) have structurally constrained support to Ukraine across the Biden, Trump, and prior administrations, because global defense commitments to multiple theaters (Europe, Asia-Pacific, Gulf) exceed current production capacity -- a decade-old, bipartisan, unresolved problem.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A structural, multi-administration capacity shortfall in munitions/interceptor production is a direct, quantifiable investment thesis for the US defense-industrial base and its suppliers, and a binding constraint on any simultaneous two-theater (Europe + Taiwan) contingency.

insights.claim: Gulf partners have reportedly declined to trade Patriot systems with Ukraine even in exchange for combat-experience data, because they fear they will not get resupplied given how far behind the US already is on existing interceptor contracts.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A concrete alliance-management symptom of the interceptor shortage -- signals real friction risk among US partners that could affect coalition cohesion in a future high-intensity conflict.

insights.claim: Providing allies only a limited quantity of an advanced weapons system (e.g., Patriot, HIMARS) lets the adversary study and adapt to it until it becomes less effective over time, comparable to stopping antibiotics early and breeding a 'superbug' -- Dara's framework for why partial, under-resourced Western support has repeatedly failed to shift the battlefield balance in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model -- 'partial-dose' military aid breeds adversary adaptation rather than decisive advantage -- for evaluating whether future incremental (vs. front-loaded) arms transfers to Taiwan or other partners are likely to be effective.
insights.quote: it's like if you get streped throat and you go to the doctor and they give you a week's worth of penicellin and you stop taking it after day two because you feel better

insights.claim: Russia is deliberately holding back excess military capacity -- additional mobilization potential, spare armor, spare drones and missiles -- rather than surging to force a breakthrough in Ukraine, because Putin is managing the war's casualty tempo to stay below the threshold that would trigger domestic unrest, while calculating he can simply wait out the Trump administration's term for a more favorable deal.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: A high-conviction, contrarian-to-consensus read (Russia is not exhausted, it is rationing effort for political control) that argues against expecting a near-term Russian military collapse or negotiated end driven by battlefield exhaustion.
insights.quote: I think he's waiting out the Trump team. That's that's what I think he's doing. What can I get from this group?

insights.claim: Ukraine's ability to endure stems in part from being on what Dara calls 'death ground' -- Russia's war aims include erasing Ukrainian identity through child abduction, forced Russification, and rape as a weapon of war, leaving Ukraine no viable option except continued resistance, unlike a war where capitulation would merely mean paying tribute.
insights.speaker: Dara
insights.so_what: Frames Ukrainian resistance durability as existential rather than merely political, implying Ukraine's willingness to fight is unlikely to erode even under severe material strain -- relevant to duration assumptions for reconstruction and frontier-risk investment.

insights.claim: Contrary to a common press narrative that Iran's domestic unrest (from the mass protests and repression earlier in the year) constrains its willingness to keep fighting, Ari argues domestic tension is not a limiting factor at all -- because the moment fighting stops, Iranian leaders must confront the unsolved economic and social crisis that caused the unrest, continued low-grade conflict lets them indefinitely postpone that reckoning.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A genuinely against-consensus call (explicitly disagreeing with other analysts) that domestic crisis makes Iran's leadership less rather than more eager to end the war -- important for anyone pricing a near-term Iran ceasefire or de-escalation as the 'obvious' outcome of internal pressure.
insights.quote: to me the domestic tensions within Iran are not a limiting factor. Actually, they're not constraining Iran. They're not going to limit Iran's decision space when it comes to the war.

insights.claim: The US and Israel diverge sharply on how the Iran conflict should end: Israel, under Netanyahu, treats the Iranian regime as an existential threat and wants to keep pushing toward regime change, while the US views Iran only as a regional threat and has no comparable appetite for continued escalation -- creating a persistent alliance-management tension inside the coalition prosecuting the war.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: A live coalition fault line (Israel wants more, the US wants an exit) that could produce divergent unilateral actions -- relevant for handicapping surprise Israeli strikes even if a nominal US-brokered de-escalation is in place.

insights.claim: The deal announced weeks before this recording was supposed to end the war, resolve Iran's nuclear program, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but Ari says it accomplished none of those things and was predictably hollow from the outset, leaving the Trump administration with no good options besides an unsatisfying declared 'win' and withdrawal, or an unwanted ground escalation.
insights.speaker: Ari
insights.so_what: Flags that the nominal Iran 'deal' referenced in current headlines is substantively empty, implying continued on/off cyclical escalation with Iran rather than durable resolution -- a caution against pricing in de-escalation as settled.

insights.claim: Unlike Russia and Ukraine's vast territory, Taiwan cannot hide from a Chinese invasion in open land, but it does have one of the densest urban environments in the world, giving it the option to attrit the PLA through urban defense or hide its leadership in dense cities to drag out the conflict long enough for outside intervention.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Identifies urban-defense capability (not open-territory attrition) as Taiwan's core protraction lever -- relevant for assessing which categories of Taiwanese defense procurement (urban/asymmetric vs. conventional platforms) actually reduce invasion risk.

insights.claim: Taiwan has for years invested heavily in large conventional platforms (ships likely to never leave harbor, manned aircraft likely destroyed on cratered airfields in the opening hours of war) partly because such big-ticket US defense-industrial purchases were seen as 'intervention insurance' -- buying goodwill with US appropriators and their districts -- rather than prioritizing the cheaper asymmetric weapons (mines, drones) that would actually be survivable and effective.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: A direct critique of Taiwan's historical arms-procurement mix -- implies continued political/lobbying pressure toward big-platform US defense sales even where asymmetric systems would better reduce actual invasion risk, a relevant dynamic for both Taiwanese defense policy and US defense contractors.
insights.quote: the Taiwanese seem to approach their weapons acquisitions from the United States as if they were purchasing intervention insurance rather than focusing on the kind of asymmetric weapons that would be most needed.

insights.claim: China has its own protraction vulnerabilities: it is heavily export-dependent and imports a large share of the oil that 'keeps the lights on' through the Strait of Malacca, a chokepoint that could be shut down, and Beijing's own push to build overseas military capability stems directly from its awareness of this long-conflict weakness.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Strait of Malacca energy-import dependence is a specific, trackable Chinese vulnerability that could be leveraged in a protracted Taiwan conflict -- relevant to Chinese energy-security policy and to war-risk premia on Malacca-route shipping and insurance.

insights.claim: China has good reason to doubt Washington's willingness to sustain a costly, casualty-heavy intervention over Taiwan, given how the US has responded to casualties and protraction in the Iran conflict with an upcoming election looming -- even though the US retains far greater material global capacity than China, recent US alienation of allies and fraying alliance cohesion undercuts its ability to isolate China economically in a protracted fight.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Directly bears on the credibility of US extended deterrence over Taiwan -- if China's calculus increasingly assumes US political will won't hold through a protracted, costly fight, that materially raises invasion probability and should be weighted in Taiwan/semiconductor-supply-chain tail-risk models.

insights.claim: Most bombed populations tend to unite rather than side with their attacker, and Taiwan is fighting for its political existence with no illusions about what capitulation would mean -- meaning that if Taiwan can organize an effective defense, the island could plausibly hold out significantly longer than Beijing expects, buying time for external intervention.
insights.speaker: Julia
insights.so_what: Pushes back against a purely pessimistic Taiwan-falls-fast base case -- a factor that should temper worst-case, near-immediate-capitulation scenarios in semiconductor and regional supply-chain contingency planning.
